body:
Start with Section III’s classical window tables and coherent lookup circuits if the table address or lookup operation is unfamiliar.

Turn two coordinates into the next point

Purpose. Specify the point-addition map and affine formulas that the register schedule must implement.

All coordinates lie in \(\mathbb F_p\), with \(p=2^{256}-2^{32}-977\) and coordinate width \(n=256\). The address \(j\) selects a known classical table entry coherently; it is not measured. The formulas below require nonzero division and multiplication operands, with exceptions listed at the end.

For accumulator \(A=(x_1,y_1)\) and table point \(T_j=(x_2,y_2)\), the coherent operation is \(|j,A\rangle\mapsto|j,A+T_j\rangle\). The selector is preserved. With arithmetic modulo \(p\), set \(\Delta x=x_1-x_2\), \(\Delta y=y_1-y_2\), and \(\lambda=\Delta y/\Delta x\). The affine formulas are \[x_3=\lambda^2-x_1-x_2,\qquad y_3=\lambda(x_2-x_3)-y_2.\] The construction arranges them so that two coordinate registers suffice; every temporary value is cleared.

Why a gcd circuit appears inside point addition

Purpose. Explain why computing the slope requires a modular inverse, and why a recorded gcd can apply that inverse.

The slope requires \(\lambda=\Delta y(\Delta x)^{-1}\pmod p\). For nonzero Δx, extended Euclid finds \(a\Delta x+bp=1\), hence \(a=(\Delta x)^{-1}\pmod p\). For example, \(3\cdot5-2\cdot7=1\) gives \(5^{-1}=3\pmod7\).

The gcd itself is already known to be 1; the useful output is the reduction history that applies the inverse. The paper records binary-gcd decisions and replays them on Δy, producing the slope in place without storing a separate inverse. Follow the division → inverse → gcd derivation.

Quantum division circuit: how recorded gcd steps turn Δy into the slope, with clean workspace.

Follow the two live registers

Purpose. Reuse the two coordinate registers by changing their meaning at each step, rather than retaining every intermediate result.

The recorded-gcd method divides the second register directly, without storing a separate inverse. The useful intermediate is \(x_2-x_3\): multiplying it by the slope removes that slope from the live state.

OperationFirst registerSecond register
Subtract table coordinates\(\Delta x\)\(\Delta y\)
Divide\(\Delta x\)\(\lambda\)
Add \(3x_2\); subtract square\(x_2-x_3\)\(\lambda\)
Multiply\(x_2-x_3\)\(y_3+y_2\)
Remove offsets; negate x\(x_3\)\(y_3\)

Release workspace; keep track of its phase

Purpose. Release table coordinates before expensive arithmetic, paying for reloads and phase corrections instead of keeping them live.

Holding table coordinates throughout both multiplications costs another \(2n\) qubits. Instead, load them when needed and measure their outputs in the X basis. For X-readout mask \(m\), where \(m\cdot f(j)\) is the binary inner product with the loaded bits and \(\alpha_j\) are normalized amplitudes, the conditioned normalized state is \[\sum_j\alpha_j|j,f(j)\rangle\longrightarrow\sum_j\alpha_j(-1)^{m\cdot f(j)}|j\rangle.\] The output register is freed, but its phase must be repaired. The first and third lookups use the same coordinates, so their masks combine by XOR; the \(3x_2\) lookup contributes its own correction.

Measurement frees the qubits; feedforward preserves coherence

Purpose. Explain how measurement, reset and feedforward jointly free qubits without destroying address coherence.

The cleanup above is measurement-based uncomputation. Measure the loaded coordinate bits in X, retain the outcome m, and reset the measured qubits. This releases up to 512 coordinate qubits before modular division. The operation transfers a known phase to j, which must be repaired; it never measures j.

For a copied control the phase repair is Z, and for an AND ancilla it is CZ. For coordinate bits F(j), the correction \((-1)^{m\cdot F(j)}\) generally requires another lookup; it is not just Pauli tracking. See the step-by-step proof and the phase-lookup circuit.

Two randomizations, two purposes

Purpose. Use offsets to avoid identity table entries and to support failure bounds; these randomizations serve different purposes.

Move the table away from infinity

For a \(w\)-bit scalar window at position \(i\), store \([j2^{iw}+\mu_i]P\). Here \(P\) is the generator and \(\mu_i\) a classical scalar offset modulo its order; choose it to exclude \(\mathcal O\). All scalar branches receive the same fixed group shift, preserving which oracle outputs coincide.

Make the square target uniform

A classical field mask \(R\) gives \((z+R)-\lambda^2-R=z-\lambda^2\). It supports the short-carry failure bound. Store \(3x_2+R\) directly in the table.

Where this saving stops

Purpose. State the resource gain together with the exceptional inputs and approximation failures that limit its guarantee.

Write \(T=T_j\) for the selected point. The generic branch excludes \(A\in\{\mathcal O,T,-T,-[2]T\}\). The last case makes \(x_2-x_3=0\), preventing reversible slope removal. Approximate arithmetic and phase repair have additional failure probabilities, analyzed in Appendix B.

The arithmetic comparison uses about \(1.196\times10^6\) Toffoli-type operations per addition, excluding three lookups, and 28 expensive additions: \(28(1.196\times10^6+3\cdot2^{16})\approx39.0\times10^6\). This uses the largest observed count in 100 runs under its executed-gate convention. The fully compiled circuit instead has 40,420,330 Toffoli injections and 1457 logical qubits.

It largely follows Schrottenloher’s register-sharing construction; IonQ changes the arithmetic primitives and table offsets. The key tradeoff is extra lookups and phase repair in exchange for reusable workspace.
title: V. High-level implementation of point addition

body:
Why point addition needs a gcd computation

Purpose. Connect this optimization to point addition: the slope needs division, and gcd reductions provide the operations that apply an inverse.

The gcd is used to perform division modulo p. It is separate from the table lookup: lookup supplies a known point’s coordinates; point addition then needs the slope between that point and the accumulator.

For accumulator \((x_1,y_1)\) and selected table point \((x_2,y_2)\), first form \(\Delta x=x_1-x_2\) and \(\Delta y=y_1-y_2\). On the nonexceptional branch,

\[\lambda=\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}=\Delta y\,(\Delta x)^{-1}\pmod p.\]

Because p is prime and \(\Delta x\ne0\pmod p\), \(\gcd(\Delta x,p)=1\). Extended Euclid finds integers a,b with

\[a\Delta x+bp=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a\Delta x=1\pmod p\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=(\Delta x)^{-1}\pmod p.\]

For example, \(3\cdot5-2\cdot7=1\), so \(5^{-1}=3\pmod7\). Thus if \(\Delta x=5\) and \(\Delta y=4\), the slope is \(4\cdot3=5\pmod7\).

The desired output is the quotient, not the gcd. The gcd is already known to be 1 on valid inputs. The useful information is the sequence of reductions that yields the inverse. The paper uses a recorded binary gcd, built from comparisons, swaps, subtractions and halving, rather than general integer division.

Its Dialog representation records those branch decisions coherently and replays them on the numerator, implementing

\[|\Delta x\rangle|\Delta y\rangle|0\rangle_{\rm work}\longmapsto|\Delta x\rangle|\Delta y(\Delta x)^{-1}\bmod p\rangle|0\rangle_{\rm work}.\]

This applies the inverse without keeping a separate 256-qubit inverse register. The denominator is preserved and temporary history is cleared. The optimized gcd representation below makes those reductions cheaper. Inputs with zero denominator are exceptional and belong to the separate failure analysis.

Open the modular-division circuit before following the optimized iteration. It shows record construction, the gate sequence that transforms the numerator, a complete register trace, and record cleanup.

Change what is stored, then simplify the gate

Purpose. Identify the expensive operation in the inherited gcd step before changing its stored variables.

Here \(p=2^n-c\) is an odd prime and \(x\) is a nonzero residue modulo \(p\). Gcd remainders \(u,v\) are integers; replay registers use field arithmetic modulo \(p\). A stored branch bit allows a step to be reversed without measuring the input.

Binary gcd records the branches used to reduce \((p,x)\) to \((1,0)\). Replaying them later performs in-place multiplication or division. With odd \(u\), parity \(a=v\bmod2\), and the operands already oriented, an ordinary step is \[v'=\frac{v-au}{2}.\] It chooses subtraction or no subtraction. The paper changes coordinates so that both branches use the same adder, with opposite signs.

An odd register exposes the next parity

Purpose. Derive the paper’s shifted representation, which makes parity updates simple and both arithmetic branches use one signed adder.

Store \(\widetilde v=v+(1-a)u\), which is always odd, and retain \(a\) in history. Since \(\widetilde v-u=2v'\), \[a'=v'\bmod2=\widetilde v[1]\oplus u[1].\] Here bit 1 is the coefficient of two. Both low bits are one, so subtraction introduces no borrow into bit 1. Restoring the odd representation gives the key identity: \[\boxed{\widetilde v'=\frac{\widetilde v+(-1)^{a'}u}{2}.}\]

Ordinary inputStored inputParity from bit 1Stored update
\((3,8)\)\((3,11)\)\(1\oplus1=0\)\((11+3)/2=7\)
\((3,5)\)\((3,5)\)\(1\oplus0=1\)\((5-3)/2=1\)

The next orientation decision is \(m=a'[u>\widetilde v']\); a bracketed predicate is one when true and zero otherwise. Only the odd branch needs this comparison. Record \(m\) before swapping so the step remains reversible.

One adder supplies both signs

Purpose. Explain the gate saving: controlling the sign of an addition can cost less than controlling whether it happens at all.

For a width-\(w\) arithmetic register (not a scalar lookup window), let \(J(z)=2^w-1-z\). Then \[J(J(z)+u)=z-u\pmod{2^w}.\] Conditional complements around an ordinary adder select addition or subtraction. They use CNOTs; the nonlinear carries need no extra control.

For field-valued replay registers \(r,s\) (here \(r\) is not a group order), use \(\widetilde s=s-(1-a)r\) and the partner update \(\widetilde s'=\widetilde s-(-1)^{a'}r\pmod p\). Its full schedule also includes modular halves or doubles and recorded swaps.

The prime-modulus boundary still matters

Purpose. Check that cheap bitwise complements implement the intended modular operation despite the special prime’s boundary cases.

For \(p=2^n-c\), bit complement obeys \(J(z)\equiv-z+(c-1)\pmod p\). The shift cancels when conjugating an exact modular adder. However, \(c-1\) canonical inputs have \(J(z)\ge p\): correct residues can become noncanonical bit strings. The implementation counts this boundary and approximately handles \(x+y=p\) with a \(0\leftrightarrow p\) swap.

Exact identities; finite arithmetic windows

Purpose. Separate exact algebraic identities from truncated implementations whose rare failures must be included in the resource estimate.

The variable change and parity XOR are exact. Table X chooses a statistical iteration budget \(1.413n+2.4\sqrt n\), shrinking width \(n-i/1.413+2.3\sqrt n\) at iteration index \(i\), comparison width \(40+2.3\sqrt n\), 37 special-case rounds, 65-bit correction windows, and 32-bit phase comparisons. Integer rounding and clipping must be specified. Million-sample tests found 21 failures in each multiplication/division direction, including phase and uncleared-workspace failures; these are statistical observations, not worst-case guarantees.

title: VI. Optimized binary gcd iteration

body:
Subtract a square without destroying its input

Purpose. Define the reversible square-subtract operation so the circuit’s output and preserved input are unambiguous.

Here \(x,y\) are \(n\)-bit field registers and \(p=2^n-c\) is an odd prime; secp256k1 has \(n=256\), \(c=2^{32}+977\). An integer square needs up to \(2n\) bits. Its exact scratch computation is separate from the approximately implemented modular update of \(y\).

Point addition needs \(|x,y\rangle\mapsto|x,y-x^2\bmod p\rangle\). Preserving \(x\) makes the map reversible. Three savings compose: pair equal cross terms, replace controlled additions by signed additions, then split the square into half-width pieces.

Use the triangle of distinct bit products

Purpose. Avoid computing both copies of each off-diagonal bit product when the two multiplication operands are identical.

For \(x=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}2^ix_i\), with binary digits \(x_i\), the diagonal satisfies \(x_i^2=x_i\), while \((i,j)\) and \((j,i)\) contribute equally: \[x^2=\sum_i2^{2i}x_i+\sum_{i<j}2^{i+j+1}x_ix_j.\] Define \(h_i=\lfloor x/2^{i+1}\rfloor\), the input above bit \(i\).

Make every step add or subtract

Purpose. Rewrite the square so each step selects an addition or subtraction, enabling the cheaper inherited adder technique.

Using \(2x_i=(2x_i-1)+1\) and summing the extra terms gives \[\sum_i2^{2i+1}h_i=\sum_jx_j(2^{2j}-2^j),\] so \[\boxed{x^2=-x+\sum_i(2x_i-1)2^{2i+1}(h_i+x_i).}\] Initialize with \(-x\); update at bit offset \(2i+1\). The control chooses the sign rather than whether the carry circuit runs.

ControlSource presented to subtractorTarget change modulo \(2^w\)
\(x_i=0\)\(h_i\)\(-h_i\)
\(x_i=1\)\(2^w-1-h_i\)\(h_i+1\)

Let the active window shrink

Purpose. Count the saving from shorter active additions rather than treating every step as a full-width operation.

The target windows have lengths \(n+1,n,\ldots,2\). A CNOT extends the current sign before each of the first \(n-1\) updates; the final update is one CNOT. With \(w-1\) Toffoli-type operations per width-\(w\) adder, \[T(n)=n+\sum_{i=0}^{n-2}(n-i)=\frac{n(n+3)}2-1.\] This counts the exact integer squarer alone, before reversal or modular accumulation.

Why sign extension matters: \(1101_2=-3\) becomes \(11101_2=-3\) when a high bit is exposed. Extending with zero would change the value to 13.

Exploit the shape of the modulus

Purpose. Combine smaller squares with the special modulus to avoid a general full-width modular reduction.

For even \(n\), let \(B=2^{n/2}\), \(x=x_L+Bx_H\), and \(p=2^n-c\). Then \(B^2\equiv c\), and \(2x_Lx_H=(x_L+x_H)^2-x_L^2-x_H^2\) yields \[-x^2\equiv(B-1)x_L^2+(B-c)x_H^2-B(x_L+x_H)^2\pmod p.\] The sum of the halves needs one extra bit.

Compute each square, accumulate its indicated multiple, and uncompute before reusing scratch. The sum-square also restores the enlarged half-register afterward. At 256 bits, the leaves have widths 128, 128, and 129; computing and reversing them costs \(2[2T(128)+T(129)]=50{,}558\), excluding the remaining additions.

The leaf squares and split identity are exact. Approximation enters in short modular carry windows and phase comparisons. Since \(c=2^{32}+2^{10}-2^6+2^4+1\), its multiples use five signed shifts, including explicit corrections for bits crossing position 255. Appendix A shows those corrections and their failure bound.

title: VII. Modular squaring

body:
The appendix supplies the arithmetic contracts

Purpose. Identify the exact input/output contracts before analyzing the approximations used to implement them.

Use \(p=2^n-c\), \(n=256\), \(c=2^{32}+977\). Here \(q\in\{0,1\}\) is a preserved control, \(\sigma\in\{-1,+1\}\) is a sign, and \(t\) is a bit offset. The local slice width \(w\) need not equal the scalar-window width 16.

AlgorithmsContract
4–6Randomize tables; loop over scalar windows; add one selected point.
7Preserve \(x,q\); update \(y\mapsto y-qx^2\pmod p\).
8: AddSlicePreserve source and control; add a signed shifted slice.
9: PhaseGEPreserve comparison inputs; apply the predicate as a sign.
10–11Accumulate structured multiples \(Bs\) and \(cs\).

The table offsets exclude infinity and add the same fixed group shift to every scalar branch. The optimized schedule uses width 16, an initial lookup, and additional classical recovery in place of three final additions, leaving 28 expensive additions. Section V gives the live-register trace.

A short update can miss a long carry

Purpose. Show how limiting the carry range saves work but can change the arithmetic result.

Let \(a=s_{[o,o+w)}\) be the width-\(w\) source slice starting at bit \(o\). For sign \(\sigma\), and control \(q\), AddSlice targets \[v'\equiv v+q\sigma2^ta\pmod p.\] Below the top boundary, it touches only \([t,t+w+\rho)\). Here \(\rho\) counts padding bits; \(\kappa\) later counts low modular-correction bits and \(\delta\) counts high comparison bits. Padding absorbs typical carries; a carry escaping that window is a failure.

Carry boundary: updating a four-bit local window \(0010+0011=0101\) is exact. Updating \(1111+0011=1\,0010\) loses the leading carry if the next bit is untouched.

Fold overflow back into low bits

Purpose. Use the special prime to replace large overflow terms with smaller low-bit corrections.

If an addition crosses the \(n\)-bit boundary, retain overflow \(h\). Since \(2^n\equiv c\pmod p\),

Before folding

\(v+a=z+h2^n\)

After folding

\(z+hc\pmod p\)

The \(c\)-correction uses only \(\kappa\) low bits, so its own escaping carry is also counted. Subtraction conjugates the positive-adder block by \(F(v)=p-1-v\), implemented by adding \(c\) then complementing: \(F(F(v)+a)=v-a\pmod p\) on its valid branches.

A correct integer can still have the wrong sign

Purpose. Explain why measured carry cleanup needs phase repair even when the integer output is correct.

X-measuring the overflow gives phase \((-1)^{mh}\). When \(m=1\), the top-wrap branch applies \((-1)^q\) and a phase comparison on the top \(\delta\) bits to erase it. PhaseGE exactly applies \((-1)^{q[x\ge y]}\) to the supplied prefixes.

Equal prefixes can hide unequal full values: \(101000_2<101011_2\), although both three-bit prefixes are \(101\). This can cause a phase error without changing any output bit.

Shifts need their overflow correction too

Purpose. Account for modular overflow when implementing multiplication by powers of two through shifts.

With \(B=2^{n/2}\) and \(s=s_L+Bs_H\), \(Bs\equiv Bs_L+cs_H\). For secp256k1, \(c=2^{32}+2^{10}-2^6+2^4+1\). Its five signed shifts lose a combined high contribution \[h_s=s_{[224,256)}+s_{[246,256)}-s_{[250,256)}+s_{[252,256)}.\] Algorithm 11 adds the missing \(ch_s\), computes it exactly in 65 bits because \(0\le h_s\le c-3\), then clears that scratch.

Assemble the bound

Purpose. Combine the component reductions into the square-subtract operation and its error accounting.

Algorithm 7 reuses these helpers for the three-square identity. With \(\rho=\delta=32\), \(\kappa=65\), 16 local additions, nine wrapping additions, and 26 complement sites, \[p_{\rm sq}\le\left(1+\frac cp\right)\left(\frac{16}{2^\rho}+\frac{35c}{2^\kappa}+\frac9{2^\delta}+\frac{9c}{2^{256}}\right)<2^{-26.59}.\] This requires the uniform random target mask and the stated helper conditions.

summary: This appendix specifies the reversible arithmetic used in the implementation. Its purpose is to expose where short carry ranges, modular corrections and phase repair enter, so the cost reductions can be matched to their failure bounds.
title: Appendix A. Algorithms

body:
Store the computation instead of its inverse

Purpose. Explain how storing reduction history avoids a separate inverse and supports in-place arithmetic.

Let \(p\) be an odd prime, \(n\) its bitlength, \(x\in\mathbb F_p^*\), and \(y\in\mathbb F_p\). The target map preserves \(x\) and replaces \(y\) by \(xy\bmod p\); its inverse replaces \(y\) by \(x^{-1}y\bmod p\).

Schrottenloher supplies the arithmetic baseline: 1462 logical qubits, including a 16-bit window, and about \(2^{25.78}\) Toffoli-type operations for secp256k1. Its central saving is a binary-gcd record that supports direct multiplication or division while sharing space with shrinking inputs. IonQ changes its controlled additions and squaring, then compiles the resulting circuit into a physical schedule.

Each gcd step has a small reversible record

Purpose. Specify the small set of branch decisions needed to reverse an integer gcd step.

Starting at \((u,v)=(p,x)\), record \(a=v\bmod2\) and \(m=a[u>v]\). Swap when \(m=1\), subtract \(au\) from \(v\), then halve \(v\). The endpoint is \((1,0)\) for nonzero \(x\) modulo prime \(p\).

Record constructionIts inverse
Swap if \(m=1\)Double the second register
Subtract \(au\)Add \(au\) back
Halve the even resultReverse the recorded swap

Write \(\rho_x\) for the history together with its fixed endpoint. The history and endpoint reconstruct the input. No branch information is discarded and no modular inverse register is built.

Apply the history to another vector

Purpose. Use the same recorded operations on another operand to perform multiplication or division.

Replay the inverse record on field registers \((r,s)=(y,0)\): for each reversed symbol, double \(s\), add \(ar\), then swap if \(m=1\). Linearity makes the endpoint \((0,xy)\pmod p\). Forward replay performs division. The complete contract is \[|x,y\rangle\longrightarrow|\rho_x,y\rangle\longrightarrow|\rho_x,xy\rangle\longrightarrow|x,xy\rangle.\] The last step reverses record construction, restoring \(x\) and clearing its history. The Dialog lesson proves the matrix identity.

Three decisions fit in five qubits

Purpose. Compress valid history patterns rather than allocate a full independent bit for every decision.

Only \((a,m)=00,10,11\) occur: an even second register never triggers a swap. Three symbols therefore have \(3^3=27\le2^5\) states. The five-Toffoli circuit below compresses six wires into five while clearing the last wire.

Promised-subspace example: \((11)(00)(10)=110010\mapsto011010\). The final zero is reusable; the first five bits distinguish this history. The encoding is a reversible permutation, not ordinary base-three notation.

The shrinking values pay for the growing history

Purpose. Reuse space released by shrinking remainders to hold the growing record.

As gcd remainders lose high bits, their now-zero storage holds new decisions. Statistical padding is essential: a bit cannot be reused while it may still contain value information. The chosen budget is near \(1.413n+2.4\sqrt n\), with \(2.3\sqrt n\) width padding. Compression gives leading history size \((5/3)(1.413n)\approx2.355n\). Adding the two replay registers gives \(4.355n+O(\sqrt n)\) qubits before additional adder workspace.

Where approximation enters

Purpose. Identify the deliberate approximations that save gates and therefore require a failure budget.

High-bit comparisons can tie while full values differ. Short pseudo-Mersenne corrections can miss escaping carries. X-measured workspace needs comparison-dependent phase repair. The iteration and width choices also reflect input statistics, rather than worst-case gcd theorems. IonQ's new odd-register update and squarer change these failure sites, so the predecessor's numerical success observations cannot simply be reused.

title: Reference [2]. Schrottenloher’s arithmetic construction

body:
Pay for the AND once

Purpose. Define the clean-ancilla AND map before discussing its computation and measurement-based inverse.

Here \(a,b\) are bits, \(ab\) is Boolean AND, and \(\oplus\) is XOR. The maps extend linearly to superpositions. Later \(n\) is adder width; the quoted count assumes zero incoming carry and discards carry-out.

A temporary AND maps \(|a,b,0\rangle\mapsto|a,b,ab\rangle\). Gidney computes it with four T resources, uses its value, then erases it through measurement with zero further T resources. The saving requires a clean target and later access to the relevant controls; it is not a replacement for a Toffoli acting on an arbitrary target.

The four-T computation

Purpose. Give the actual non-Clifford construction rather than treating the AND as a free operation.

Let \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), \(S=T^2\), and \(|T\rangle=T|+\rangle\). This redraw of Gidney's Figure 3 uses one input magic state, one T gate, and two \(T^\dagger\) gates: four T resources in total. The remaining gates are Clifford.

Erase information without erasing coherence

Purpose. Prove how the measured outcome determines the phase correction needed to restore coherence.

X-measuring the AND ancilla with outcome \(m\) produces \[\sum_{a,b}\alpha_{ab}|a,b,ab\rangle\longrightarrow\sum_{a,b}\alpha_{ab}(-1)^{mab}|a,b\rangle.\] A conditional \(\mathrm{CZ}^m\) removes exactly that phase, independently of the amplitudes.

Control branchPhase when \(m=1\)CZ correctionNet phase
\(00,01,10\)\(+1\)\(+1\)\(+1\)
\(11\)\(-1\)\(-1\)\(+1\)

Without the correction, input \(|++\rangle\) retains uniform computational-basis probabilities but acquires an entangling sign on \(|11\rangle\). Testing only the output bits would miss this failure.

One nonlinear computation per carry

Purpose. Use temporary ANDs for carry generation so each nonlinear carry is paid for only once.

For bits \(a_i,b_i\) and incoming carry \(c_i\), the sum is \(s_i=a_i\oplus b_i\oplus c_i\). The next carry is \[c_{i+1}=c_i\oplus[(a_i\oplus c_i)(b_i\oplus c_i)].\] The bracket is one temporary AND; everything around it is XOR.

No incoming carry

\(c_i=0\Rightarrow c_{i+1}=a_ib_i\). Both input bits must be one.

Incoming carry

\(c_i=1\Rightarrow c_{i+1}=1\oplus(1-a_i)(1-b_i)\). Either input bit suffices.

The cost moves into workspace and measurements

Purpose. State the workspace and measurement costs that accompany the lower non-Clifford gate count.

Without retained carry-out, an n-bit Gidney adder uses \(n-1\) temporary ANDs: \(4n-4\) T resources and \(n-1\) measurement erasures. IonQ counts this as \(n-1\) Toffoli-type computations. Carry ancillas remain occupied until erasure; less workspace requires a different adder or a hybrid.

Zero additional T cost does not mean zero physical time. Measurement, classical correction, and access to the controls still need scheduling. This is why IonQ compiles the Clifford and measurement work instead of estimating duration from magic-state injections alone. Conditional complements extend the same adder to add-or-subtract without doubling its nonlinear carry work.

body:
The task: divide without storing an inverse

Purpose. Define modular division and explain why applying an inverse directly can save a temporary field register.

Fix a known odd prime p. The quantum input contains a nonzero denominator \(x\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}\) and a numerator \(y\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\), possibly in superposition. We want

\[|x\rangle|y\rangle\longmapsto|x\rangle|yx^{-1}\bmod p\rangle.\]

For elliptic-curve addition, x is the difference of the two x-coordinates, y is the difference of the two y-coordinates, and the quotient is the slope. Here x,y denote field elements, not curve points. The inverse exists because \(\gcd(p,x)=1\).

Dialog stores the sequence of gcd reductions, then applies that sequence to another operand. It thereby applies \(x^{-1}\) without holding the inverse in a separate register.

What the record contains

Purpose. Specify the branch decisions that form the record, so replay is an explicit reversible operation rather than an undefined instruction.

Start two integer remainders at \((u,v)=(p,x)\). The following ordinary binary-gcd convention keeps u odd. While v is nonzero:

  1. Set the swap bit \(m_i=1\) if v is odd and v<u, otherwise 0; swap u,v when it is 1.
  2. Set the subtraction bit \(a_i=v\bmod2\) using v after that swap.
  3. Replace \(v\leftarrow(v-a_i u)/2\). The numerator is even, so this is exact integer halving.

The process ends at (1,0). Its record \(R(x)\) is the ordered list of pairs \((m_i,a_i)\), together with which steps are active. In a quantum circuit these bits are computed reversibly and remain coherent with x. Use a fixed-length schedule, with completed branches padded by identity operations; no measurement determines when a branch stops.

Three blocks, with explicit contracts

Purpose. Show the complete division circuit and define what each block consumes, preserves and clears.

Besides x, use a record register R and two field registers s,t, initially \(R=0,s=0,t=y\). “0” means an all-zero register. The boxes below mean exactly:

BoxAction
Make record\(|x,0\rangle\mapsto|x,R(x)\rangle\): reversibly compute the denominator’s gcd decisions, preserving x.
Apply recordUse the stored decisions as controls on s,t. Starting from (0,y), the result is \((yx^{-1},0)\). The next drawing expands one step.
Erase recordReverse Make record: \(|x,R(x)\rangle\mapsto|x,0\rangle\). It does not act on the quotient.

Open “Apply record”

Purpose. Expand replay into controlled swaps, subtraction and modular halving using decisions already computed from the denominator.

For each active pair \((m_i,a_i)\), apply the same swap, subtraction and halving to s,t. Crucially, the decisions come from R(x); do not recompute them from s,t.

Replay arithmetic is modulo p. For a canonical value \(0\le t<p\), modular halving is

\[h_p(t)=\begin{cases}t/2,&t\text{ even},\\(t+p)/2,&t\text{ odd},\end{cases}\qquad h_p(t)=2^{-1}t\pmod p.\]

This is reversible because doubling modulo p is its inverse. It is not a bit shift that discards the low bit. The subtraction and halving boxes include their own clean arithmetic workspace.

Why these steps produce the quotient

Purpose. Prove that the recorded linear transformations send the numerator to its quotient; the matrices are proof notation, not stored data.

For a fixed x, its stored decisions specify a linear map on a pair of values. Call the matrix of step i \(M_i\), and the product in execution order \(M_x=M_L\cdots M_1\), where L is the number of active steps. In the field,

\[M_i=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-a_i&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}^{m_i}.\]

First, gcd reduction takes (p,x) to (1,0). Reducing this identity modulo p gives

\[M_x\binom0x=\binom10.\]

Second, \((0,y)^T=(yx^{-1})(0,x)^T\). By linearity,

\[M_x\binom0y=yx^{-1}M_x\binom0x=\binom{yx^{-1}}0.\]

The circuit executes the recorded operations; it does not store or multiply by a dense matrix. The matrix is only a way to prove what replay does. Reversing replay instead maps \((y,0)\) to \((0,xy)\), giving multiplication.

One record, followed all the way through

Purpose. Check the complete mechanism on one small division, including every intermediate register value.

Take \(p=13,x=5,y=4\). Left: generate the record from integer remainders. Right: apply it modulo 13 to the numerator pair. Each row follows one complete step.

Step(mᵢ,aᵢ)Remainders (u,v)Replay (s,t)
Start—(13,5)(0,4)
1(1,1)(5,4)(4,11)
2(0,0)(5,2)(4,12)
3(0,0)(5,1)(4,6)
4(1,1)(1,2)(6,12)
5(0,0)(1,1)(6,6)
6(0,1)(1,0)(6,0)

In the first replay step, swap (0,4) to (4,0), subtract to (4,9) modulo 13, then halve 9 as \((9+13)/2=11\). The final quotient is 6, verified by \(5\cdot6=4\pmod{13}\).

Why the quantum record must be cleared

Purpose. Remove the denominator-dependent history coherently so it cannot retain information about the quantum input.

After replay, R(x) is still correlated with the denominator. Directly measuring it could reveal x. Reversing Make record clears it coherently using the unchanged x, while leaving the quotient untouched. All temporary registers finish at zero, so they carry no information about the input. Internal measurement-based cleanup is possible only with its phase corrections.

What makes this a space-saving representation

Purpose. Explain the actual storage saving: history occupies space freed by shrinking remainders, beyond merely avoiding an explicit inverse.

The drawing keeps x and R separate to explain correctness. Dialog instead stores history in space freed as the gcd remainders shrink. After replay, reversing that representation change restores x and clears the record. The benefit comes from this shared storage, not from treating the record as free.

Reference [52] introduces Dialog for polynomial arithmetic. Schrottenloher adapts the approach to integer binary gcd, and IonQ further changes the stored variables to reduce adder costs. The circuit here explains the exact ordinary-variable mechanism; the paper’s truncated schedules and approximate arithmetic require its separate failure bounds.

Next: how IonQ makes each gcd step cheaper. Return to the slope calculation in point addition.

body:
Put the control on complements instead of carries

Purpose. Move the control to bitwise complements so the carry circuit can remain unconditional.

Let \(n\) be register width, \(u,z\) be unsigned \(n\)-bit integers, and \(b\) a preserved control bit. Add–subtract selects a sign; add–skip selects whether to add. Carry-out means retaining an extra overflow bit.

Let \(A_u(z)=z+u\pmod{2^n}\), preserving the source \(u\), and let \(J(z)=2^n-1-z\). Direct substitution gives \[J A_u J(z)=z-u\pmod{2^n}.\] Conditional complements around an ordinary adder therefore select addition or subtraction coherently. Each complement is a fan of CNOTs; the nonlinear carry circuit receives no extra control.

The control choice changes the non-Clifford count

Purpose. Compare the nonlinear costs of selecting a sign and selecting whether an addition occurs.

Operation in this adder familyNo carry-outCarry-out retained
Add\(n-1\)\(n\)
Add or subtract\(n-1\)\(n\)
Add or skip\(2n-1\)\(2n+1\)

Entries count Toffoli-type computations under the stated ancilla conventions. The extra CNOTs still occupy physical connections and schedule time.

Recover an ordinary product from signed additions

Purpose. Recover ordinary multiplication from a sequence of signed additions plus a known correction.

Writing \(x=\sum_i2^ix_i\), replace each selected contribution by a signed one: \[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(2x_i-1)2^iy=2xy-(2^n-1)y.\] Add the known correction \((2^n-1)y\) and halve to recover \(xy\). Every step now runs an adder; the bit selects its sign.

What changed: bit \(x_i=0\) now contributes \(-2^iy\), while \(x_i=1\) contributes \(+2^iy\). The correction accounts for all former zero branches at once.

Unsigned carry-out introduces a second correction

Purpose. Track finite-register offsets so the signed algebra remains correct in an unsigned implementation.

The carry-out circuit represents subtraction as \(z+2^n-y\). Step \(i\) therefore contributes \[(1-x_i)2^{n+i}+(2x_i-1)2^iy.\] Summing gives \(R=2xy+2^{2n}-2^n(x+1+y)+y\). The following corrections turn \(R\) into \(2xy\), after which a wire relabeling halves it. Treating these intermediate registers as signed integers without their offsets would give the wrong product.

The resulting multiplier, and what IonQ imports

Purpose. State the resulting multiplication cost and distinguish the imported technique from IonQ’s adaptations.

The full integer construction costs \(n^2+4n+3\), compared with \(2n^2+n\) for the reference controlled-adder multiplier. Modulo \(2^n\), discarding high contributions gives \(n^2/2+3n/2\), versus \(n^2\). These are counts for specific circuits.

IonQ imports the signed non-modular arithmetic, rather than Litinski's entire windowed Montgomery-reduction construction. It specializes equal inputs into a squarer and separately handles the secp256k1 modulus.

The squarer pairs equal off-diagonal products: \[x^2=\sum_i2^{2i}x_i+\sum_{i<j}2^{i+j+1}x_ix_j.\] Combining that symmetry with signed control gives \(n(n+3)/2-1\) Toffoli-type operations. The gcd optimization reaches the same primitive through \(\widetilde v=v+(1-a)u\). Each application needs its own identity; replacing add-or-skip in an unchanged algorithm would not preserve its result.

body:
Recover two cross terms from one product

Purpose. Derive the three-product identity that removes one of the four half-size products.

Take even bitlength \(n\), radix \(B=2^{n/2}\), and halves \(0\le x_L,x_H,y_L,y_H

Split \(x=x_L+Bx_H\) and \(y=y_L+By_H\). Ordinary multiplication uses four half-size products. Karatsuba forms only three: \[z_0=x_Ly_L,\quad z_2=x_Hy_H,\quad z_1=(x_L+x_H)(y_L+y_H).\] The combined cross term is \(z_1-z_0-z_2=x_Ly_H+x_Hy_L\), hence \[\boxed{xy=z_0+B(z_1-z_0-z_2)+B^2z_2.}\]

Direct expansion

Two diagonal products plus two cross products.

Karatsuba expansion

Two diagonal products plus one product of sums; additions recover both cross terms.

One split can be better than full recursion

Purpose. Explain why arithmetic overhead and workspace can make a single split preferable to full recursion.

Recursion gives \(M(n)=3M(n/2)+O(n)\), so the multiplication exponent falls from 2 to \(\log_2 3\approx1.585\). Each level also costs additions, workspace, and quantum cleanup. IonQ uses one split, with exact 128- and 129-bit schoolbook squarers at the leaves.

The product of sums becomes a square

Purpose. Specialize the identity to squaring so its leaves are smaller squares rather than general products.

Set \(y=x\). Then \[x^2=x_L^2+B[(x_L+x_H)^2-x_L^2-x_H^2]+B^2x_H^2.\] The half-sum can reach \(2B-2\), so it requires one more bit than either half. This is why one leaf is 129 bits rather than 128.

Fold the high square through the modulus

Purpose. Exploit the modulus to fold the high part into cheaper low-width corrections.

For \(B=2^{n/2}\) and \(p=2^n-c\), substitute \(B^2\equiv c\pmod p\) and negate: \[-x^2\equiv(B-1)x_L^2+(B-c)x_H^2-B(x_L+x_H)^2\pmod p.\] This exact identity specifies the three target updates. Its coefficients are shifts and short multiples, matching the modulus.

Reuse scratch only after reversing the square

Purpose. Clear each temporary square before reusing its storage, preserving the coherent input.

Each leaf follows compute, accumulate, uncompute. Scratch holding \(f(x)\) is entangled with the preserved input; measuring it in the computational basis would reveal information about \(x\). Reversing its computation frees the register coherently.

StageSource half-registerSquare scratch
Prepare the sum\(x_H\to x_H+x_L\)\(0\)
Compute; update target\(x_H+x_L\)\((x_H+x_L)^2\)
Reverse square; subtract \(x_L\)\(x_H\)\(0\)

The enlarged half-register's extra bit also returns to zero. The first two leaves use the same scratch lifecycle without preparing a sum.

Count the leaves separately from their accumulation

Purpose. Count both the smaller squares and the arithmetic needed to accumulate and reduce them.

With \(T(m)=m(m+3)/2-1\), the leaf counts are 8383, 8383, and 8513. Computing and reversing all three costs \(50{,}558\) Toffoli-type operations. This subtotal excludes half-sum preparation, shifted multiples, modular corrections, and scheduling.

Approximation enters the modular target updates through short carries and truncated phase comparisons. It does not enter the Karatsuba identity or the integer leaf squares. Keeping the exact identity separate from those implementations makes both resource and failure accounting auditable.
